arXiv:1107.1595v1 [math.AP] 08 Jul 2011

Global existence for the Euler-Maxwell system

P. Germain    N. Masmoudi
Abstract

The Euler-Maxwell system describes the evolution of a plasma when the collisions are important enough that each species is in a hydrodynamic equilibrium. In this paper we prove global existence of small solutions to this system set in the whole three-dimensional space, by combining the space-time resonance method, dispersive estimates, localization estimates and energy estimates. An important novelty is that we can prove a very slow growth (tC​ϵt^{C\epsilon}) of high derivatives even with only 1t\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} decay of the L∞L^{\infty} norm by reiterating the energy estimate.

1 Introduction

1.1 Plasma physics and Euler-Maxwell

There are different models to describe the state of a plasma depending on several parameters such as the Debey length, the plasma frequency, the collision frequencies between the different species… Formal derivation of these models can be found in Plasma Physics textbooks (see for instance Bellan [1], Boyd and Sanderson [4], Dendy [8] and the paper [2] …)

Since the plasma consists of a very large number of interacting particles, it is appropriate to adopt a statistical approach to describe it. In the kinetic description, it is only necessary to evolve the distribution function fα​(t,x,v)f_{\alpha}(t,x,v) for each species in the system. Vlasov equation is used in this case with the Lorentz force term and a collision term. It is coupled with the Maxwell equations for the electromagnetic fields.

If collisions are important, then each species is in a local equilibrium and the plasma is treated as a fluid. More precisely it is treated as a mixture of two or more interacting fluids. This is the two-fluid model or the so-called Euler-Maxwell system. We refer to [23, 16, 21] for more about hydrodynamic limits. Another level of approximation consists in treating the plasma as a single fluid by using the fact that the mass of the electrons is much smaller than the mass of the ions. This is the model which we are going to consider in this paper.

1.2 The Euler-Maxwell equation

The Cauchy problem for the one fluid version of the Euler-Maxwell system reads

{ρ(∂tu+u⋅∇u)=−p′​(ρ)m∇ρ−e​ρm(E+1cu×B)∂tρ+∇⋅(ρ​u)=0∂tB+c∇×E=0∂tE−c∇×B=4πeρu∇⋅E=4​π​e​(ρ¯−ρ)∇⋅B=0(u,ρ,E,B)​(t=0)=(u0,ρ0,E0,B0).\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\rho\left(\partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u\right)=-\frac{p^{\prime}(\rho)}{m}\nabla\rho-\frac{e\rho}{m}\left(E+\frac{1}{c}u\times B\right)\\ \partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho u)=0\\ \partial_{t}B+c\nabla\times E=0\\ \partial_{t}E-c\nabla\times B=4\pi e\rho u\\ \nabla\cdot E=4\pi e(\bar{\rho}-\rho)\\ \nabla\cdot B=0\\ (u,\rho,E,B)(t=0)=(u_{0},\rho_{0},E_{0},B_{0}).\end{array}\right. (1.1)

The unknown functions are: ρ\rho, the density of electrons; uu, the average velocity of the electrons; EE, the electric field; BB the magnetic field. The physical constants are: cc, the speed of light; ee, the charge of the electron; mm, the mass of the electron. Finally, ρ¯\bar{\rho} is the uniform density of ions, and the electron gas is supposed to be barotropic, the pressure being given by p⁡(ρ)p(\rho).

Let us first recall a few results related to (1.1). Global existence of weak solutions was obtained for a related 1d model in [5] using compensated compactness. Also, several asymptotic problems (WKB asymptotics, incompressible limit, non-relativistic limit, quasi-neutral limit…) were studied to derive simplified models starting from the Euler-Maxwell system [31, 33, 32, 28]. We also refer to [25] where the incompressible Navier-Stokes system is studied.

Going back to our system (1.1), we notice that the two last equations above can be removed, as soon as they are satisfied at the initial time, which we assume from now on: they are then conserved by the flow given by the first four.

1.3 Vicinity of the trivial equilibrium state

An obvious equilibrium state of the above system is (ρ,u,E,B)=(ρ¯,0,0,0)(\rho,u,E,B)=(\bar{\rho},0,0,0). In order to study its stability, it is instructive to linearize the above system, and compute evolution equations for its unknowns. It is convenient then to split uu into its divergence-free part P​uPu, and its curl-free part Q​uQu: u=P​u+Q​uu=Pu+Qu. Similarly, E=P​E+Q​EE=PE+QE. The obtained system reads

{(∂t2−cs2Δ+ωp2)(Q​Eρ−ρ¯Q​u)=0(∂t2−c2Δ+ωp2)(P​E∇×B+4​π​e​ρ¯c​P​u)=0∂t(B−c​me∇×u)=0\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\left(\partial_{t}^{2}-c_{s}^{2}\Delta+\omega_{p}^{2}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}QE\\ \rho-\bar{\rho}\\ Qu\end{array}\right)=0\\ \left(\partial_{t}^{2}-c^{2}\Delta+\omega_{p}^{2}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}PE\\ \nabla\times B+\frac{4\pi e\bar{\rho}}{c}Pu\end{array}\right)=0\\ \partial_{t}\left(B-\frac{cm}{e}\nabla\times u\right)=0\\ \end{array}\right.

where the speed of sound csc_{s} and the plasma frequency ωp\omega_{p} are given by

cs=p′​(ρ¯)mandωp=4​π​e2​ρ¯m.c_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{p^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})}{m}}\;\;\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\;\;\omega_{p}=\sqrt{\frac{4\pi e^{2}\bar{\rho}}{m}}.

Thus around the equilibrium, and at a linear level, some unknowns are governed by Klein Gordon equation (with different speeds), whereas the quantity B−c​me∇×uB-\frac{cm}{e}\nabla\times u is conserved. The Klein Gordon equations entail decay, which is one of the keys of the global stability result which we will prove; as for the quantity B−c​me∇×uB-\frac{cm}{e}\nabla\times u, no decay is to be expected a priori. We will therefore set it to zero, which, as it turns out, is conserved by the nonlinear flow.

1.4 Adimensionalization and reductions

In the following, we set for simplicity the physical constants mm, ee, cc, as well as ρ¯\bar{\rho} to 1. We also drop the 4​π4\pi factors, since they are irrelevant. However cs2=p′​(ρ¯)=p′​(1)c_{s}^{2}=p^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})=p^{\prime}(1) remains a number less than 1. In order to simplify a little bit the estimates, we assume

p⁡(ρ)​=d​e​f​cs23​ρ3.p(\rho)\overset{def}{=}\frac{c_{s}^{2}}{3}\rho^{3}.

Finally, set

n​=d​e​f​ρ−1.n\overset{def}{=}\rho-1.

The Cauchy problem becomes

(E​M){∂tu+u⋅∇u=−cs2ρ∇ρ−E−u×B∂tρ+∇⋅(ρ​u)=0∂tB+∇×E=0∂tE−∇×B=ρ​u∇⋅E=−n∇⋅B=0(u,n,E,B)​(t=0)=(u0,n0,E0,B0).(EM)\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u=-c_{s}^{2}\rho\nabla\rho-E-u\times B\\ \partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho u)=0\\ \partial_{t}B+\nabla\times E=0\\ \partial_{t}E-\nabla\times B=\rho u\\ \nabla\cdot E=-n\\ \nabla\cdot B=0\\ (u,n,E,B)(t=0)=(u_{0},n_{0},E_{0},B_{0}).\end{array}\right.

We shall furthermore assume that, initially,

B=∇×u.B=\nabla\times u. (1.2)

This condition is conserved by the flow of the above system: in order to see this, use the identity u⋅∇u=−u×(∇×u)+∇|u|22u\cdot\nabla u=-u\times(\nabla\times u)+\nabla\frac{|u|^{2}}{2} to compute

∂t(B−∇×u)=∇×(u⋅∇u+u×B)=∇×(−u×(∇×u)+∇|u|22)−∇×(u×B)=∇×(u×(B−∇×u)).\begin{split}\partial_{t}(B-\nabla\times u)&=\nabla\times\left(u\cdot\nabla u+u\times B\right)\\ &=\nabla\times\left(-u\times(\nabla\times u)+\nabla\frac{|u|^{2}}{2}\right)-\nabla\times(u\times B)\\ &=\nabla\times\left(u\times(B-\nabla\times u)\right).\end{split}

The linearized system reads now

{(∂t2−cs2Δ+1)(Q​unQ​E)=0(∂t2−Δ+1)(P​uP​EB)=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\left(\partial_{t}^{2}-c_{s}^{2}\Delta+1\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}Qu\\ n\\ QE\end{array}\right)=0\\ \left(\partial_{t}^{2}-\Delta+1\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}Pu\\ PE\\ B\end{array}\right)=0.\end{array}\right. (1.3)

1.5 Obtained results

Prior to stating our theorem, we need to define the operator A​=d​e​f​⟨D⟩|D|A\overset{def}{=}\frac{\langle D\rangle}{|D|} (see Section 2 for the precise definition of this operator).

Theorem 1.1.

Assume that the resonance separation condition 4.1 holds; it is the case generically in csc_{s}. Fix α0>0\alpha_{0}>0. Then there exists C0,ϵ0,N0>0C_{0},\epsilon_{0},N_{0}>0 such that: if ϵ<ϵ0\epsilon<\epsilon_{0}, N>N0N>N_{0} and

‖⟨x⟩1+α0​(u0,A​n0,E0,A​B0)‖HN<ϵ,\left\|\langle x\rangle^{1+\alpha_{0}}(u_{0},An_{0},E_{0},AB_{0})\right\|_{H^{N}}<\epsilon,

then there exists a unique global solution of (E​M)(EM) such that

supt[⟨t⟩−C0​ϵ​‖(u,A​n,E,A​B)​(t)‖HN+⟨t⟩​‖(u,A​n,E,A​B)​(t)‖3]≲ϵ.\sup_{t}\left[\langle t\rangle^{-C_{0}\epsilon}\|(u,An,E,AB)(t)\|_{H^{N}}+\sqrt{\langle t\rangle}\|(u,An,E,AB)(t)\|_{3}\right]\lesssim\epsilon.

Furthermore, it scatters as tt goes to infinity in that there exists a solution (uℓ,nℓ,Eℓ,Bℓ)(u_{\ell},n_{\ell},E_{\ell},B_{\ell}) of the linear system (1.3) corresponding to intial data in HN−2H^{N-2} such that

‖(u,n,E,B)​(t)−(uℓ,nℓ,Eℓ,Bℓ)​(t)‖HN−2→0as t→∞.\left\|(u,n,E,B)(t)-(u_{\ell},n_{\ell},E_{\ell},B_{\ell})(t)\right\|_{H^{N-2}}\rightarrow 0\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\mbox{as $t\rightarrow\infty$}.
Remark 1.2.

A few observations on the hypotheses on the initial data:

  • —

    The requirements on A​n0An_{0} and A​B0AB_{0} imply necessarily that ∫n0=\int n_{0}= and ∫B0=0\int B_{0}=0. In particular this is consistent with the electric neutrality.

  • —

    We did not try to optimize the number of derivatives in L2L^{2} required (NN), but rather aimed at a proof as simple as possible. On the other hand, the weight appearing above (⟨x⟩1+α\langle x\rangle^{1+\alpha}) seems nearly optimal; a more precise analysis would maybe allow ⟨x⟩\langle x\rangle instead of ⟨x⟩1+α\langle x\rangle^{1+\alpha}.

The proof will be essentially split into two parts: controling the HNH^{N} norm of (u,n,E,B)(u,n,E,B); and proving the decay in various norms. The former is achieved by an energy estimate; and the latter by the method of space-time resonances, which was introduced in [12]. It was also used to prove global existence of small data solutions for water waves [13, 14].

1.6 Stability of compressible Euler and related models in dimension 3

It is instructive to compare the above results to earlier works on compressible Euler in dimension 3, or couplings of compressible Euler with various fields (electrostatic, electromagnetic, gravitational…). For all these models, a fundamental question is whether given data lead to blow up or a global solution.

A first class of results gives blow up for various types of data. The fundamental work is due to Sideris [30], who proved finite time blow up for compressible Euler; he was able to obtain this result for data arbitrarily close to the equilibrium state given by a zero velocity, and a constant density. Many results followed: finite time blow up was showed for the compressible Euler equation with compactly supported data by Makino, Ukai, and Kawashima [22]; for the attractive Euler-Poisson equation with compactly supported data by Perthame [27]; for the repulsive Euler-Poisson equation with compactly supported data by Makino and Perthame [24]; and for the relativistic compressible Euler equation by Guo and Tahvildar-Zadeh [19] and Pan and Smoller [26].

All of the aforementioned results rely on a non-constructive proof, and do not say much about the nature of the singularity. Recently, Christodoulou [6] was able to describe in a very precise manner the blow up process for the relativistic compressible Euler equation.

Another line of research gives global existence (and scattering) for data close to the equilibrium state given by constant density, and all the fields (including the velocity) equal to zero. Such of result was first obtained by Guo [17] for repulsive Euler-Poisson; and by Guo and Pausader [18] for the ion dynamics in Euler-Maxwell. In both cases, the curl of the data is assumed to be zero, and this condition is conserved by the flow of the equation. Finally, global existence for Euler-Maxwell with relaxation was obtained by Duan [9].

Focusing on the case of small data (i.e. close to an equilibrium), some common features emerge from the results which have been mentioned. Global existence is only known under the assumption that the flow is irrotational: this eliminates a mode which is linearly non-decaying. Under this assumption, a crucial point is then the nature of the linearized equation: roughly speaking, blow up may occur if it is a wave equation, whereas global existence is expected if it is a Klein-Gordon equation. The relevant difference between these two situations is that the latter gives a decay ∼1t3/2\sim\frac{1}{t^{3/2}}, whereas the former only decays ∼1t\sim\frac{1}{t}.

In the case of Euler-Maxwell, which is treated in this paper, the condition B=∇×uB=\nabla\times u is also meant to restrict the solution to the subspace along which the linearized problem is governed by Klein-Gordon equations. The novelty is that these Klein-Gordon equations have different speeds, making the nonlinear interaction more intricate.

3 A formulation adapted to energy estimates

Our aim here is to rewrite the equation in such a way that its dispersive properties become more transparent, but energy estimates can also be easily obtained.

Split

(unEB)=(Q​unQ​E0)+(P​u0P​EB)​=d​e​f​Va+Vp\left(\begin{array}[]{l}u\\ n\\ E\\ B\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{l}Qu\\ n\\ QE\\ 0\end{array}\right)+\left(\begin{array}[]{l}Pu\\ 0\\ PE\\ B\end{array}\right)\overset{def}{=}V_{a}+V_{p}

where VpV_{p} contains the unknowns which (in the linearization (1.3)) propagate as electromagnetic waves, and VaV_{a} the unknowns which (still in the linearization (1.3)) propagate as acoustic waves.

3.1 The acoustic system

We focus here on the evolution of Va=(Q​u,n,Q​E, 0)V_{a}=\left(Qu\,,\,n\,,\,QE\,,\,0\right). It is governed by the system

{∂tQu=−QE−∇|u|22−cs2ρ∇ρ∂tn=−∇⋅(ρu)∇⋅E=−n.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}Qu=-QE-\nabla\frac{|u|^{2}}{2}-c_{s}^{2}\rho\nabla\rho\\ \partial_{t}n=-\nabla\cdot(\rho u)\\ \nabla\cdot E=-n.\end{array}\right.

In order to diagonalize this system, let us switch to the unknown function

𝒜=12​(⟨D⟩cs|D|​n+i​∇|D|⋅u)\mathcal{A}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}{|D|}n+i\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\cdot u\right)

Q​u=−2​∇|D|​ℑ​𝔪​𝒜andn=2​|D|⟨D⟩cs​ℜ​𝔢​𝒜.Qu=-2\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\mathfrak{Im}\mathcal{A}\;\;\;\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\;\;\;n=2\frac{|D|}{\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}\mathfrak{Re}\mathcal{A}.

The evolution of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is given by

2​∂t𝒜=2​i​⟨D⟩cs​𝒜−⟨D⟩cs∇|D|⋅(n​u)+i​|D|2​(|u|2+cs2​|n|2).2\partial_{t}\mathcal{A}=2i\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}\mathcal{A}-\frac{\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}\nabla}{|D|}\cdot(nu)+\frac{i|D|}{2}\left(\left|u\right|^{2}+c_{s}^{2}|n|^{2}\right). (3.1)

3.2 The Maxwell (or electromagnetic) system

{∂tB=−∇×E∂tP​E=∇×B+P⁡(ρ​u)\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}B=-\nabla\times E\\ \partial_{t}PE=\nabla\times B+P(\rho u)\end{array}\right.

which implies

∂t2B−ΔB+B=−∇×(nu).\partial_{t}^{2}B-\Delta B+B=-\nabla\times(nu).

∂tℬ−i⟨D⟩ℬ=−∇|D|×(nu),\partial_{t}\mathcal{B}-i\langle D\rangle\mathcal{B}=-\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\times(nu),

and the original unknown functions P​uPu, P​EPE and BB can be recovered by

Pu=∇|D|​⟨D⟩×ℑ𝔪ℬ,PE=−∇|D|×ℜ𝔢ℬandB=|D|⟨D⟩ℑ𝔪ℬ.Pu=\frac{\nabla}{|D|\langle D\rangle}\times\mathfrak{Im}\mathcal{B}\;\;\;\;,\;\;\;\;PE=-\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\times\mathfrak{Re}\mathcal{B}\;\;\;\;\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\;\;\;\;B=\frac{|D|}{\langle D\rangle}\mathfrak{Im}\mathcal{B}.

The Euler-Maxwell system now reads

(E​M′){∂t𝒜−i⟨D⟩cs𝒜=−12⟨D⟩∇|D|⋅(nu)+14i|D|(|u|2+|n|2)∂tℬ−i⟨D⟩ℬ=−∇|D|×(nu)(𝒜,ℬ)​(t=0)=(𝒜0,ℬ0)(EM^{\prime})\quad\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\mathcal{A}-i\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}\mathcal{A}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\langle D\rangle\nabla}{|D|}\cdot(nu)+\frac{1}{4}i|D|\left(\left|u\right|^{2}+|n|^{2}\right)\\ \partial_{t}\mathcal{B}-i\langle D\rangle\mathcal{B}=-\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\times(nu)\\ (\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})(t=0)=(\mathcal{A}_{0},\mathcal{B}_{0})\end{array}\right.

with

{Q​u=−2​∇|D|​ℑ​𝔪​𝒜n=2​|D|⟨D⟩cs​ℜ​𝔢​𝒜P​u=∇|D|​⟨D⟩×ℑ​𝔪​ℬ.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}Qu=-2\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\mathfrak{Im}\mathcal{A}\\ n=2\frac{|D|}{\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}\mathfrak{Re}\mathcal{A}\\ Pu=\frac{\nabla}{|D|\langle D\rangle}\times\mathfrak{Im}\mathcal{B}.\end{array}\right.

𝒜0=d​e​f12(⟨D⟩cs|D|n0+i∇|D|⋅u0)andℬ0=−∇|D|×E0+i⟨D⟩|D|B0.\mathcal{A}_{0}\overset{def}{=}\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}{|D|}n_{0}+i\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\cdot u_{0}\right)\;\;\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\;\;\mathcal{B}_{0}=-\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\times E_{0}+i\frac{\langle D\rangle}{|D|}B_{0}.

a⁡(t)​=d​e​f​e−i​t​⟨D⟩cs​𝒜​(t)andb⁡(t)​=d​e​f​e−i​t​⟨D⟩​ℬ​(t).a(t)\overset{def}{=}e^{-it\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}\mathcal{A}(t)\;\;\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\;\;b(t)\overset{def}{=}e^{-it\langle D\rangle}\mathcal{B}(t).

4 A formulation adapted to decay estimates

As we saw, the system (E​M′)(EM^{\prime}) written above is equivalent to (E​M)(EM); it will be the correct formulation to perform energy estimates. However, as far as dispersive estimates go, we will not need all the structure of (E​M′)(EM^{\prime}): only resonances will play an important rôle. It will be convenient to write (E​M′)(EM^{\prime}) in a more compact form.

4.1 Duhamel’s formula in Fourier space

Writing Duhamel’s formula in terms of aa and bb gives

{a(t)=𝒜0+∫0te−i​s​⟨D⟩cs[−12⟨D⟩∇|D|⋅(nu)+14i|D|(|u|2+|n|2)]dsb⁡(t)=ℬ0−∫0te−i​s​⟨D⟩​[∇|D|×(n​u)]​ds.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}a(t)=\mathcal{A}_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-is\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}\left[-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\langle D\rangle\nabla}{|D|}\cdot(nu)+\frac{1}{4}i|D|\left(\left|u\right|^{2}+|n|^{2}\right)\right]\,ds\\ b(t)=\mathcal{B}_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}e^{-is\langle D\rangle}\left[\frac{\nabla}{|D|}\times(nu)\right]\,ds.\end{array}\right.

Taking the Fourier transform gives

{a^​(t,ξ)=𝒜0^​(ξ)+“nonlinear term”b^​(t,ξ)=ℬ0^​(ξ)+“nonlinear term”.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\widehat{a}(t,\xi)=\widehat{\mathcal{A}_{0}}(\xi)+\mbox{``nonlinear term''}\\ \widehat{b}(t,\xi)=\widehat{\mathcal{B}_{0}}(\xi)+\mbox{``nonlinear term''}.\end{array}\right.

In order to make notations lighter and estimates easier, we will now give up some of the structure of the above system.

4.2 Space-time resonances in the context of Euler-Maxwell

Seeing (4.1) as an oscillatory integral, it becomes clear that the cancellation properties of ϕ\phi and ∂ηϕ\partial_{\eta}\phi will provide a key to understanding the large time behaviour of our system: this is the idea of space time resonances. See [11] for a general presentation, and [10] for the case of (semilinear) Klein-Gordon equations with different propagation speeds.

Recall that the phase functions corresponding to all possible quadratic interactions are given by

ϕk,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2​(ξ,η)​=d​e​f​⟨ξ⟩k+ϵ1​⟨η⟩ℓ+ϵ2​⟨ξ−η⟩m\phi^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m}(\xi,\eta)\overset{def}{=}\langle\xi\rangle_{k}+\epsilon_{1}\langle\eta\rangle_{\ell}+\epsilon_{2}\langle\xi-\eta\rangle_{m} (4.3)

Next define for each interaction the space, time, and space-time resonant sets

𝒮k,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2​=d​e​f​{(ξ,η)|ϕk,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2=0}(”space resonances”)𝒯k,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2​=d​e​f​{(ξ,η)|∂ηϕk,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2=0}(”time resonances”)ℛk,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2​=d​e​f​𝒮k,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2∩𝒯k,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2.(”space-time resonances”)\begin{split}&\mathcal{S}^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m}\overset{def}{=}\{(\xi,\eta)\,|\,\phi^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m}=0\}\;\;\;\;\;\;\mbox{(''space resonances")}\\ &\mathcal{T}^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m}\overset{def}{=}\{(\xi,\eta)\,|\,\partial_{\eta}\phi^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m}=0\}\;\;\;\;\;\;\mbox{(''time resonances")}\\ &\mathcal{R}^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m}\overset{def}{=}\mathcal{S}^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m}\cap\mathcal{T}^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m}.\;\;\;\;\;\;\mbox{(''space-time resonances")}\end{split}

The set of all space-time resonances is

ℛ=∪ϵ1,ϵ2,k,ℓ,mℛϵ1,ϵ2k,ℓ,m;\mathcal{R}=\cup_{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2},k,\ell,m}\mathcal{R}^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m};

it is compact and hence it is bounded. We denote by Cℛ−1C_{\mathcal{R}}-1 the radius of a ball that contains ℛ\mathcal{R}. Finally, define the outcome and germ, or source frequencies for space-time resonances: these are simply the projections of ℛk,ℓ,mϵ1,ϵ2\mathcal{R}^{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}}_{k,\ell,m} in the ξ\xi variable, respectively the union of the projections in the η\eta and ξ−η\xi-\eta variables. More precisely if πξ​(ξ′,η′)=ξ′\pi_{\xi}(\xi^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})=\xi^{\prime}, πη​(ξ′,η′)=η′\pi_{\eta}(\xi^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})=\eta^{\prime} and πξ−η​(ξ′,η′)=ξ′−η′\pi_{\xi-\eta}(\xi^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})=\xi^{\prime}-\eta^{\prime}, we set

𝒪​=d​e​f​πξ​(ℛ)𝒢​=d​e​f​πη​(ℛ)∪πξ−η​(ℛ).\begin{split}&\mathcal{O}\overset{def}{=}\pi_{\xi}\left(\mathcal{R}\right)\\ &\mathcal{G}\overset{def}{=}\pi_{\eta}\left(\mathcal{R}\right)\cup\pi_{\xi-\eta}\left(\mathcal{R}\right).\end{split}
Definition 4.1.

Space-time resonances are said to be separated if no outcome frequency is also a germ frequency. In mathematical terms, 𝒢∩𝒪=∅\displaystyle\mathcal{G}\cap\mathcal{O}=\emptyset.

7 Decay estimates

We want to prove here that

supt[⟨t⟩12+3​δ1​‖(𝒜,ℬ)‖WN′′,(13−δ1)−1+⟨t⟩1−3​δ1​‖Z~𝒪​(𝒜,ℬ)‖WN′′,(16+δ1)−1+⟨t⟩​‖Z~𝒪​(𝒜,ℬ,u,n)‖∞]≲‖(ei​t​⟨D⟩cs​𝒜0+ei​t​⟨D⟩​ℬ0)‖X+‖(𝒜,ℬ)‖X2.\begin{split}&\sup_{t}\left[\langle t\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}+3\delta_{1}}\left\|(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\right\|_{W^{N^{\prime\prime},\left(\frac{1}{3}-\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}}}+\langle t\rangle^{1-3\delta_{1}}\left\|\widetilde{Z}_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\right\|_{W^{N^{\prime\prime},\left(\frac{1}{6}+\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}}}+\langle t\rangle\left\|\widetilde{Z}_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},u,n)\right\|_{\infty}\right]\\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\lesssim\left\|(e^{it\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}\mathcal{A}_{0}+e^{it\langle D\rangle}\mathcal{B}_{0})\right\|_{X}+\left\|(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\right\|_{X}^{2}.\end{split} (7.1)

7.1 Control of the WN′′,(16+δ1)−1W^{N^{\prime\prime},\left(\frac{1}{6}+\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}} and WN′′,(13−δ1)−1W^{N^{\prime\prime},\left(\frac{1}{3}-\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}} norms

The two first norms in (7.1) above can be controlled as in [10]:

  • —

    As far as the control of the WN′′,(16+δ1)−1W^{N^{\prime\prime},\left(\frac{1}{6}+\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}} norm goes, the main difference between the Euler-Maxwell system and the setting of [10] is the quasilinearity of Euler-Maxwell. This induces a further loss of regularity in the nonlinear term, which is however easily absorbed using the HNH^{N} norm.

  • —

    The estimate for the WN′′,(13−δ1)−1W^{N^{\prime\prime},\left(\frac{1}{3}-\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}} norm is a low frequency question (since it is only problematic on 𝒪\mathcal{O}). Therefore, the argument of [10] applies identically.

We do not detail these two points, and focus directly on the third norm in (7.1).

7.2 Control of the W2,∞W^{2,\infty} norm

Proceeding as in Subsection 4.1, we can derive a generic term gg corresponding to the nonlinear term in Duhamel’s formula for uu and nn. It turns out, since uu and nn are given from 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} by the action of a Fourier multiplier, that this gg would satisfy exactly the properties listed in Subsection 4.1.

Thus all we need to do is to prove that, for gg as in Subsection 4.1,

‖Z~𝒪​ei​t​⟨D⟩ℓ​g​(t)‖W2,∞≲1⟨t⟩​‖(𝒜,ℬ)‖X2.\left\|\widetilde{Z}_{\mathcal{O}}e^{it\langle D\rangle_{\ell}}g(t)\right\|_{W^{2,\infty}}\lesssim\frac{1}{\langle t\rangle}\left\|(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\right\|_{X}^{2}.

In order to prove this, we shall split Z~𝒪​ei​t​⟨D⟩ℓ​g​(t)\widetilde{Z}_{\mathcal{O}}e^{it\langle D\rangle_{\ell}}g(t) as follows

+∫1t∫χ~𝒪(ξ)χ𝒮(ξ,η)ei​s​ϕm(ξ,η)c^(s,η)c^(s,ξ−η)dηds\displaystyle+\int_{1}^{t}\int\widetilde{\chi}_{\mathcal{O}}(\xi)\chi_{\mathcal{S}}(\xi,\eta)e^{is\phi}m(\xi,\eta)\widehat{c}(s,\eta)\widehat{c}(s,\xi-\eta)\,d\eta\,ds (7.2b)

8 Localization estimates

We want to prove here that

supt[1t​‖|x|​(a,b)‖HN′+‖|x|1/8​Z~𝒪​(a,b)‖2]≲‖(ei​t​⟨D⟩cs​𝒜0,ei​t​⟨D⟩​ℬ0)‖X+‖(𝒜,ℬ)‖X2.\sup_{t}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\left\||x|(a,b)\right\|_{H^{N^{\prime}}}+\left\||x|^{1/8}\widetilde{Z}_{\mathcal{O}}(a,b)\right\|_{2}\right]\lesssim\left\|(e^{it\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}\mathcal{A}_{0},e^{it\langle D\rangle}\mathcal{B}_{0})\right\|_{X}+\left\|(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\right\|_{X}^{2}.

As above, this reduces to proving that the generic term

g⁡(t)=ℱ−1​∫0tei​s​ϕ​(ξ,η)​m​(η,ξ)​c^​(η,s)​c^​(ξ−η,s)​𝑑sg(t)=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\int_{0}^{t}e^{is\phi(\xi,\eta)}m(\eta,\xi)\widehat{c}(\eta,s)\widehat{c}(\xi-\eta,s)\,ds

defined in (4.1) satisfies the localization estimates

supt[1t​‖|x|​g‖HN′+‖|x|1/8​Z~𝒪​g‖2]≲‖(𝒜,ℬ)‖X2.\sup_{t}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\left\||x|g\right\|_{H^{N^{\prime}}}+\left\||x|^{1/8}\widetilde{Z}_{\mathcal{O}}g\right\|_{2}\right]\lesssim\left\|(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\right\|_{X}^{2}. (8.1)

By symmetry, it suffices to control

g′​(t)=ℱ−1​∫0tei​s​ϕ​(ξ,η)​m​(η,ξ)​ζ1​(ξ,η)​c^​(η,s)​c^​(ξ−η,s)​𝑑sg^{\prime}(t)=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\int_{0}^{t}e^{is\phi(\xi,\eta)}m(\eta,\xi)\zeta^{1}(\xi,\eta)\widehat{c}(\eta,s)\widehat{c}(\xi-\eta,s)\,ds

(where the cut-off symbol ζ1\zeta^{1}, defined in Section 5, ensures that |ξ−η|≲|η||\xi-\eta|\lesssim|\eta| for (ξ,η)(\xi,\eta) large). The bound for the second norm in (8.1) was derived in [10], and the same scheme of proof applies here (once again, the novelty compared to [10] is that the Euler-Maxwell system is quasilinear, but the resulting loss of regularity in the nonlinear term is easily absorbed by the HNH^{N} norm). Therefore, we focus on the first norm in (8.1), for which some new difficulties arise. It will be helpful to split mm as m=m0​m1​m2m=m_{0}m_{1}m_{2} (see Subsection 4.1). The estimate of (10.14) is exactly the same as the estimate of (10.7) and we do not detail it again.

Now, it remains to control the last term on the right-hand side of (10.5), namely the term involving the rest term. Again, if the low frequency term is non-outcome then we can estimate the term directly using the integrable L6L^{6} decay of the non-outcome part. Hence, the only difficult terms are those for which the low frequency term is outcome. The most difficult terms are very similar to those we treated above by integration by parts in time, namely (10.7) and (10.14). In addition we have terms of the type

We also have terms of the form

From Lemma 10.1, we know that ϕ\phi is always bounded away from zero in the region we are interested in, nemaly ξ\xi large and |η|≤Cℛ|\eta|\leq C_{\mathcal{R}}. Integration by parts in time yields terms that are easier to control than above. In particular the corresponding term to (10.8a) can be expressed as

=\displaystyle= −∫0t∫∫1ϕ𝒞^(η)[u⋅∇∂N−k𝒜^(ξ−η)∂N𝒜^¯(ξ)+∂N−k𝒜^(ξ−η)u⋅∇∂N𝒜^¯(ξ)]\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{t}\int\!\int\frac{1}{\phi}\widehat{\mathcal{C}}(\eta)\left[\widehat{u\cdot\nabla\partial^{N-k}\mathcal{A}}(\xi-\eta)\overline{{\widehat{\partial^{N}\mathcal{A}}}}(\xi)+\widehat{\partial^{N-k}\mathcal{A}}(\xi-\eta)\overline{{\widehat{u\cdot\nabla\partial^{N}\mathcal{A}}}}(\xi)\right] (10.17)

11 Scattering

Let us prove for instance that 𝒜\mathcal{A} scatters. We write symbolically the equation (3.1) on 𝒜\mathcal{\mathcal{A}} as

∂t𝒜−i​⟨D⟩cs​𝒜=∂𝒞​𝒞\partial_{t}\mathcal{A}-i\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}\mathcal{A}=\partial\mathcal{C}\mathcal{C}

By definition, 𝒜\mathcal{A} will scatter in HN−2H^{N-2}, say at +∞+\infty, if and only if

∫0tei​s​⟨D⟩cs​∂𝒞⁡(s)​𝒞​(s)​𝑑s\int_{0}^{t}e^{is\langle D\rangle_{c_{s}}}\partial\mathcal{C}(s)\mathcal{C}(s)ds

converges as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. By the Strichartz estimates (12.4), it suffices that the right-hand side ∂𝒞​𝒞\partial\mathcal{C}\mathcal{C} belongs to Lt(12+32​δ1)−1​([0,∞),Lx(13−δ1)−1)L_{t}^{\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}}\left([0,\infty),L_{x}^{\left(\frac{1}{3}-\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}}\right). This is the case since

‖∂𝒞​𝒞‖Lt(12+32​δ1)−1​Lx(13−δ1)−1≲‖𝒞‖X2​‖⟨t⟩C0​ϵ​⟨t⟩−12−32​δ1‖L(12+32​δ1)−1<∞,\left\|\partial\mathcal{C}\mathcal{C}\right\|_{L_{t}^{\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}}L_{x}^{\left(\frac{1}{3}-\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}}}\lesssim\left\|\mathcal{C}\right\|_{X}^{2}\left\|\langle t\rangle^{C_{0}\epsilon}\langle t\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\delta_{1}}\right\|_{L^{\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\delta_{1}\right)^{-1}}}<\infty,

where the last inequality follows since ϵ\epsilon is small enough.

12.1 Sobolev embedding theorem

If 1≤p≤q≤∞1\leq p\leq q\leq\infty and

k>3p−3q,k>\frac{3}{p}-\frac{3}{q},

then

‖f‖q≲‖f‖Wk,q.\left\|f\right\|_{q}\lesssim\left\|f\right\|_{W^{k,q}}. (12.1)

12.2 Product laws

If 1<p,r<∞1<p,r<\infty, 1≤q≤∞1\leq q\leq\infty, k≥0k\geq 0 and

1p+1q=1r,\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{r},

then

‖f​g‖Wk,r≲‖f‖Wk,p​‖g‖q+‖f‖q​‖g‖Wk,p\left\|fg\right\|_{W^{k,r}}\lesssim\left\|f\right\|_{W^{k,p}}\left\|g\right\|_{q}+\left\|f\right\|_{q}\left\|g\right\|_{W^{k,p}} (12.2)

12.3 Dispersive and Strichartz estimates

The standard dispersive estimates for Klein-Gordon can be found in Ginibre and Velo [15]

‖ei​t​⟨D⟩​f‖p≲t3p−32​‖f‖W5​(12−1p)+ϵ,p′if 2≤p≤∞ and ϵ>0.\left\|e^{it\langle D\rangle}f\right\|_{p}\lesssim t^{\frac{3}{p}-\frac{3}{2}}\|f\|_{W^{5\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p}\right)+\epsilon,p^{\prime}}}\;\;\;\;\;\;\mbox{if $2\leq p\leq\infty$ and $\epsilon>0$.} (12.3)

We need the following Strichartz estimate for the Klein-Gordon equation (see for instance Ibrahim, Masmoudi and Nakanishi [20]): if ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and 0≤δ≤130\leq\delta\leq\frac{1}{3},

‖∫0tei​s​⟨D⟩​F​(s)​𝑑s‖2≲‖F‖L(12+32​δ)−1​W(56−52​δ+ϵ),(56−δ)−1.\left\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{is\langle D\rangle}F(s)\,ds\right\|_{2}\lesssim\left\|F\right\|_{L^{\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\delta\right)^{-1}}W^{\left(\frac{5}{6}-\frac{5}{2}\delta+\epsilon\right),\left(\frac{5}{6}-\delta\right)^{-1}}}. (12.4)

For the reader familiar with Besov spaces, this estimate follows from the interpolation between

‖∫0tei​s​⟨D⟩​F​(s)​𝑑s‖2≲‖F‖L1​L2\left\|\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}e^{is\langle D\rangle}F(s)\,ds\right\|_{2}\lesssim\|F\|_{L^{1}L^{2}}

and

‖∫0tei​s​⟨D⟩​F​(s)​𝑑s‖2≲‖F‖L2​B6/5,25/6.\left\|\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}e^{is\langle D\rangle}F(s)\,ds\right\|_{2}\lesssim\left\|F\right\|_{L^{2}B^{5/6}_{6/5,2}}.

Estimates similar to the first four points above were proved in [10]. It essentially suffices to use the basic estimate

Next, we want to study a particular kind of symbol, which will not satisfy standard Coifman-Meyer bounds, but still admit Hölder-like bounds (in the bilinear case for instance, we only focus on the case L∞×L2→L2L^{\infty}\times L^{2}\rightarrow L^{2} bound, but it should be clear from the proof that more general Lp×Lq→LrL^{p}\times L^{q}\rightarrow L^{r} bounds, with 1p+1q=1r\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{r}, also hold).

μ~j​(ξ,η,ν)=ψ~​(ξ2j)​χ​(2​η)​χ​(ν2j−5)​∑k,ℓ,m∈ℤ3αk,ℓ,mj​ei​2​π​m​ξ​2−j−2​ei​2​π​k​η​ei​2​π​ℓ​ν​2−j+7,\widetilde{\mu}_{j}(\xi,\eta,\nu)=\widetilde{\psi}\left(\frac{\xi}{2^{j}}\right)\chi(2\eta)\chi\left(\frac{\nu}{2^{j}-5}\right)\sum_{k,\ell,m\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\alpha_{k,\ell,m}^{j}e^{i2\pi m\xi 2^{-j-2}}e^{i2\pi k\eta}e^{i2\pi\ell\nu 2^{-j+7}},

or, coming back to μ\mu,

μj​(ξ,η,ν)=ψ~​(ξ−η−ν2j)​χ​(2​η)​χ​(ν2j−5)​∑k,ℓ,mαk,ℓ,mj​ei​2​π​m​(ξ−η−ν)​2−j−2​ei​2​π​k​η​ei​2​π​ℓ​ν​2−j+7.\mu_{j}(\xi,\eta,\nu)=\widetilde{\psi}\left(\frac{\xi-\eta-\nu}{2^{j}}\right)\chi(2\eta)\chi\left(\frac{\nu}{2^{j}-5}\right)\sum_{k,\ell,m}\alpha_{k,\ell,m}^{j}e^{i2\pi m(\xi-\eta-\nu)2^{-j-2}}e^{i2\pi k\eta}e^{i2\pi\ell\nu 2^{-j+7}}.

Next notice that the αk,ℓj\alpha^{j}_{k,\ell} are uniformly bounded in jj, with arbitrarily quickly decaying (inverse) polynomial bounds:

for any N,supj|αk,ℓ,mj|=αk,ℓ,m≲1|(k,ℓ,m)|N.\mbox{for any $N$,}\quad\sup_{j}|\alpha^{j}_{k,\ell,m}|=\alpha_{k,\ell,m}\lesssim\frac{1}{|(k,\ell,m)|^{N}}. (12.6)

This can be seen by simply coming back to their definition:

αk,ℓ,mj=C​2−6​j​∫|ξ|≤2j+2∫|η|≤1∫|ν|≤2j−7μ~j​(ξ,η,ν)​e−i​2​π​m​ξ​2−j−2​e−i​2​π​k​η​e−i​2​π​ℓ​ν​2−j+7​𝑑ν​𝑑η​𝑑ξ=C​∫|ξ|≤1∫|η|≤1∫|ν|≤1μ~j​(2j+2​ξ,η,2j−7​ν)​e−i​2​π​m​ξ​e−i​2​π​k​η​e−i​2​π​ℓ​ν​dν​dη​dξ,\begin{split}\alpha^{j}_{k,\ell,m}&=C2^{-6j}\int_{|\xi|\leq 2^{j+2}}\int_{|\eta|\leq 1}\int_{|\nu|\leq 2^{j-7}}\widetilde{\mu}_{j}(\xi,\eta,\nu)e^{-i2\pi m\xi 2^{-j-2}}e^{-i2\pi k\eta}e^{-i2\pi\ell\nu 2^{-j+7}}\,d\nu\,\,d\eta\,d\xi\\ &=C\int_{|\xi|\leq 1}\int_{|\eta|\leq 1}\int_{|\nu|\leq 1}\widetilde{\mu}_{j}(2^{j+2}\xi,\eta,2^{j-7}\nu)e^{-i2\pi m\xi}e^{-i2\pi k\eta}e^{-i2\pi\ell\nu}\,d\nu\,\,d\eta\,d\xi,\end{split}

and the conclusion follows since the bounds (12.5) imply a uniform control (in jj) of the symbols μ~j​(2j+2​ξ,η,2j−7​ν)\widetilde{\mu}_{j}(2^{j+2}\xi,\eta,2^{j-7}\nu).

Coming back to physical space, we have achieved the following decomposition for TμT_{\mu}:

Tμ(f,g,h)=∑j,k,ℓ,mαk,ℓ,mjSj−5f(⋅+k)S0g(⋅+ℓ2−j+7)P~jh(⋅+m2−j−2).T_{\mu}(f,g,h)=\sum_{j,k,\ell,m}\alpha_{k,\ell,m}^{j}S_{j-5}f(\cdot+k)S_{0}g(\cdot+\ell 2^{-j+7})\widetilde{P}_{j}h(\cdot+m2^{-j-2}).

The desired estimates follows easily by almost orthogonality between the jj-summands

‖Tμ​(f,g,h)‖2≲∑k,ℓ,m[∑jαk,ℓ,mj‖Sj−5f(⋅+k)S0g(⋅+ℓ2−j+7)P~jh(⋅+m2−j−2)‖22]1/2≲∑k,ℓ,m[αk,ℓ,mj∥f∥∞2∥g∥∞2∑j∥P~jh(⋅+m2−j−2)∥22]1/2≲∑k,ℓ,mαk,ℓ,m​[‖f‖∞2​‖g‖∞2​‖h‖22]1/2≲‖f‖∞​‖g‖∞​‖h‖2,\begin{split}\left\|T_{\mu}(f,g,h)\right\|_{2}&\lesssim\sum_{k,\ell,m}\left[\sum_{j}\alpha_{k,\ell,m}^{j}\left\|S_{j-5}f(\cdot+k)S_{0}g(\cdot+\ell 2^{-j+7})\widetilde{P}_{j}h(\cdot+m2^{-j-2})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]^{1/2}\\ &\lesssim\sum_{k,\ell,m}\left[\alpha_{k,\ell,m}^{j}\|f\|_{\infty}^{2}\|g\|_{\infty}^{2}\sum_{j}\|\widetilde{P}_{j}h(\cdot+m2^{-j-2})\|_{2}^{2}\right]^{1/2}\\ &\lesssim\sum_{k,\ell,m}\alpha_{k,\ell,m}\left[\|f\|_{\infty}^{2}\|g\|_{\infty}^{2}\|h\|_{2}^{2}\right]^{1/2}\\ &\lesssim\|f\|_{\infty}\|g\|_{\infty}\|h\|_{2},\end{split}

where we used in the last inequality the bound (12.6). ∎

Equipped with the previous lemma, we can prove the following proposition.

Proposition 12.3.

Let MM be as in (10.12), and fix α>0\alpha>0. Then the following estimate holds:

‖TM​(f,g,h)‖2≲‖f‖W1+α,∞​‖g‖∞​‖h‖2.\left\|T_{M}(f,g,h)\right\|_{2}\lesssim\|f\|_{W^{1+\alpha,\infty}}\|g\|_{\infty}\|h\|_{2}.
Proof.

Recall that

M⁡(ξ,η,ν)=−μ⁡(ξ,η)​(η+ν)+[μ⁡(ξ,η)−μ⁡(ξ−ν,η)]​ξ​=d​e​f​M1​(ξ,η,ν)+M2​(ξ,η,ν),M(\xi,\eta,\nu)=-\mu(\xi,\eta)(\eta+\nu)+\left[\mu(\xi,\eta)-\mu(\xi-\nu,\eta)\right]\xi\overset{def}{=}M_{1}(\xi,\eta,\nu)+M_{2}(\xi,\eta,\nu),

where the operator μ\mu is supported in a strip {|η|≲1,|ξ|>>1}\{|\eta|\lesssim 1\,,\,|\xi|>>1\} and satisfies the bounds

|∂ξα∂ηβμ|≲1|ξ||α|.\left|\partial^{\alpha}_{\xi}\partial^{\beta}_{\eta}\mu\right|\lesssim\frac{1}{|\xi|^{|\alpha|}}.

We will treat separately the operators TM1T_{M_{1}} and TM2T_{M_{2}}, further distinguishing for the latter between the regions where |ξ−η−ν|≲ν|\xi-\eta-\nu|\lesssim\nu, and those where |ξ−η−ν|>>|ν||\xi-\eta-\nu|>>|\nu|, by writing

TM2​(f,g,h)=∑j≥0TM2​(Pj​f,g,Sj+10​h)+∑j≥0TM2​(Sj−10​f,g,Pj​h)up to a remainder.T_{M_{2}}(f,g,h)=\sum_{j\geq 0}T_{M_{2}}(P_{j}f,g,S_{j+10}h)+\sum_{j\geq 0}T_{M_{2}}(S_{j-10}f,g,P_{j}h)\quad\mbox{up to a remainder}.

Since the remainder is smooth and compactly supported, it is easily estimated, and we forget about it in the following in order to concentrate on the sum over jj. Notice that we overtook the Littlewood-Paley operators PjP_{j} and SjS_{j} defined in Lemma 12.2.

The operator TM1T_{M_{1}}. Simply observe that

TM1​(f,g,h)=Tμ​(∇f,g​h)+Tμ​(f,(∇g)​h).T_{M_{1}}(f,g,h)=T_{\mu}(\nabla f,gh)+T_{\mu}(f,(\nabla g)h).

Thus Lemma 12.2 gives the conclusion.

The operator TM2T_{M_{2}} in the case |ξ−η−ν|≲ν|\xi-\eta-\nu|\lesssim\nu. Recall that M2M_{2} is given by [μ⁡(ξ,η)−μ⁡(ξ−ν,η)]​ξ\left[\mu(\xi,\eta)-\mu(\xi-\nu,\eta)\right]\xi. There is no cancellation between the two summands in the range we consider, so μ⁡(ξ,η)​ξ\mu(\xi,\eta)\xi and μ⁡(ξ−ν,η)​ξ\mu(\xi-\nu,\eta)\xi can be considered separately. Since they are estimated in similar ways, we focus on the first one. Notice that Tμ⁡(ξ,η)​ξ=∇TμT_{\mu(\xi,\eta)\xi}=\nabla T_{\mu}. Using Lemma 12.2 and proceeding in a straightforward way, we get the desired estimates:

‖∑j∇Tμ​(Pj​f,g​Sj+10​h)‖2≲∑j2j​‖Tμ​(Pj​f,g​Sj+10​h)‖2≲∑j2j​‖Pj​f‖∞​‖g‖∞​‖Sj​h‖2≲‖f‖W1+α,∞​‖g‖2​‖h‖2.\begin{split}\left\|\sum_{j}\nabla T_{\mu}(P_{j}f,gS_{j+10}h)\right\|_{2}&\lesssim\sum_{j}2^{j}\left\|T_{\mu}(P_{j}f,gS_{j+10}h)\right\|_{2}\lesssim\sum_{j}2^{j}\|P_{j}f\|_{\infty}\|g\|_{\infty}\|S_{j}h\|_{2}\\ &\lesssim\|f\|_{W^{1+\alpha,\infty}}\|g\|_{2}\|h\|_{2}.\end{split}

The operator TM2T_{M_{2}} in the case |ξ−η−ν|>>ν|\xi-\eta-\nu|>>\nu. In this case, we observe that the operator

(f,g,h)↦∑jTM2​(Sj−10​f,g,Pj​h)(f,g,h)\mapsto\sum_{j}T_{M_{2}}(S_{j-10}f,g,P_{j}h)

has a symbol

M2′​(ξ,η,ν)=M2​(ξ,η,ν)​∑jψ⁡(ξ−η−ν2j)​χ​(ν2j−10)M_{2}^{\prime}(\xi,\eta,\nu)=M_{2}(\xi,\eta,\nu)\sum_{j}\psi\left(\frac{\xi-\eta-\nu}{2^{j}}\right)\chi\left(\frac{\nu}{2^{j-10}}\right)

which can be written

M2′​(ξ,η,ν)=M~2​(ξ,η,ν)⋅νwithM~2​(ξ,η,ν)​=d​e​f​∑jψ⁡(ξ−η−ν2j−10)​χ​(ν2j)​ξ​∫01∂ξμ⁡(ξ−t​ν,η)​𝑑t.M_{2}^{\prime}(\xi,\eta,\nu)=\widetilde{M}_{2}(\xi,\eta,\nu)\cdot\nu\quad\mbox{with}\quad\widetilde{M}_{2}(\xi,\eta,\nu)\overset{def}{=}\sum_{j}\psi\left(\frac{\xi-\eta-\nu}{2^{j-10}}\right)\chi\left(\frac{\nu}{2^{j}}\right)\xi\int_{0}^{1}\partial_{\xi}\mu(\xi-t\nu,\eta)\,dt.

The key observation is that, due to the hypotheses on μ\mu, we have the bound |ξ||α|​|∂ξαμ|≤C|\xi|^{|\alpha|}|\partial^{\alpha}_{\xi}\mu|\leq C and hence M~2\widetilde{M}_{2} satisfies the conditions of Lemma 12.2. The estimate follows easily:

‖TM2​(Sj​f,g,Pj​h)‖2=‖TM~2​(∇f,g,h)‖2≲‖∇f‖∞​‖g‖∞​‖h‖2.\left\|T_{M_{2}}(S_{j}f,g,P_{j}h)\right\|_{2}=\left\|T_{\widetilde{M}_{2}}(\nabla f,g,h)\right\|_{2}\lesssim\left\|\nabla f\right\|_{\infty}\left\|g\right\|_{\infty}\left\|h\right\|_{2}.

∎
